metaDescription: Own mineral rights in Spanish Valley, UT near Moab? We buy Paradox Basin and Cane Creek-area fee interests, unaffected by the area's tourism growth.
heroLead: Spanish Valley sits just south of Moab, in the part of San Juan County where a tourism-driven real estate boom has run right over the top of a mineral estate that most new residents don't know exists.
intro: Spanish Valley has changed enormously over the past two decades as Moab's outdoor recreation economy pushed housing and short-term rentals south along Highway 191. What hasn't changed is that the surface real estate market and the mineral estate underneath it are legally separate, and long-time families in the valley often still hold mineral rights their grandparents retained when they sold surface acreage to developers decades ago.

We hear from a fair number of Spanish Valley owners who assumed their mineral interest was sold along with the land at some point. It's worth checking your deed history before assuming that, because a surface sale doesn't automatically include the minerals unless the deed says so explicitly.

sections.heading: Severed minerals under developed land
paragraphs: If your family sold or subdivided property in Spanish Valley without a mineral reservation clause, the minerals went with the land. If the deed did reserve minerals, or if the family simply never sold the underlying land at all, that interest is still yours to hold or sell independently of whatever's built on the surface today.
We pull the recorded deed chain at the San Juan County recorder's office in Monticello to confirm which situation applies before discussing a number.

sections.heading: Proximity to the Cane Creek trend
paragraphs: Spanish Valley sits close to the Cane Creek shale acreage northwest of Moab that has drawn renewed horizontal drilling interest in recent years, a meaningful shift from the vertical, more sporadic activity of prior decades. Depending on your specific section, that proximity can matter to value even if there's no well directly on your tract yet.
We track current permitting in this corridor closely since it moves faster than in most other parts of San Juan County.

sections.heading: What this means for a sale decision
paragraphs: For owners weighing whether to sell now versus wait, the honest answer is that Cane Creek activity has been picking up, which argues for patience if you can afford it, but a lot of families holding small fractional interests would rather have liquid cash today than a speculative position tied to future drilling that may or may not reach their specific section.
We make an offer based on where things stand today and let you decide which side of that tradeoff makes sense for your situation.

faqs.question: Did I lose my mineral rights when my family sold land in Spanish Valley?
faqs.answer: Only if the sale deed didn't reserve minerals. Many older San Juan County deeds transferred surface and minerals together, but plenty reserved minerals separately. We check your specific deed to confirm.

faqs.question: Is Cane Creek activity actually close enough to affect my Spanish Valley interest?
faqs.answer: It depends on your section. We compare your legal description against current permitting boundaries before making that call rather than assuming proximity based on the town name alone.

faqs.question: Should I wait for more drilling before selling?
faqs.answer: That's your call to make, and we lay out both sides honestly. Waiting has upside if activity reaches your section, but a fractional interest not yet drilled also carries real uncertainty that a cash sale removes.
